stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A team led by civil engineer Rosa Iglesias tested whether recycled plastic fibers could replace some of the steel mesh used to reinforce concrete sidewalks. The test slabs that contained the highest proportion of fibers and had cured for the full twenty-eight ______ fewer surface cracks after a winter of freeze-thaw cycles than did the slabs reinforced with steel mesh alone.
explanation: The subject is long: "The test slabs that contained the highest proportion of fibers and had cured for the full twenty-eight days." Its main verb is "developed." The "that" clause is essential because it tells you which slabs the sentence means, so no comma sets it off. The "and" inside that clause joins two verbs that share one subject ("contained ... and had cured"), so that doesn't call for punctuation either. Nothing should come between a subject and its verb, so the version with no punctuation is correct.

B.why: The subject is long, so you put a comma where you would pause to breathe. A comma can't separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is. Cross out the "that" clause and you get "The test slabs, developed fewer surface cracks," which is clearly wrong.

C.why: You treated the text before the blank as a setup for what follows. A colon has to come after a complete sentence, though, and "The test slabs that contained ... twenty-eight days" is only a subject with no main verb. The colon would cut the subject off from its verb.

D.why: You used a semicolon as if two complete sentences meet at the blank. Neither side can stand alone: the left side is a subject without a main verb, and the right side is a verb phrase without a subject. A semicolon between two fragments is never correct.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When a mid-sized river city rezoned its downtown parking garages for housing, critics predicted that shoppers would abandon the district. The opposite happened. A study published four years after the change found that the number of people arriving on foot, by bicycle, or by streetcar on an average weekday ______ by nearly a third, while ground-floor vacancies along the main commercial corridor fell to their lowest level in two decades.
explanation: The subject is the long noun phrase "the number of people arriving on foot, by bicycle, or by streetcar on an average weekday," and its verb is "had risen." No punctuation goes between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is. You can check this by crossing out the middle: "the number ... had risen by nearly a third" reads as one clean clause.

B.why: You put a comma between the verb "had risen" and the phrase "by nearly a third" that completes it. The long subject before the blank makes the sentence feel like it needs a pause, but nothing here calls for a comma.

C.why: A semicolon has to join two complete sentences. "By nearly a third, while ground-floor vacancies ... fell" is a phrase followed by a dependent clause, so it can't stand alone, and the semicolon is wrong.

D.why: A colon introduces an explanation or a list. "By nearly a third" just finishes the verb, so the colon cuts the sentence apart at a point where the grammar has no break.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Glacial meltwater does not always flow straight to the sea. Some of it seeps into thick beds of gravel and moves underground for months before it reappears. To follow that hidden path, hydrologist Ines Varga added a harmless fluorescent dye to a meltwater stream in the Swiss Alps. Over the next eleven weeks, her team recorded ______ the dye at springs as far as nine kilometers downslope.
explanation: "Recorded" is a verb that needs an object, and "the faint traces of the dye" is that object. No punctuation goes between a verb and its object. Without punctuation, the sentence reads as a single main clause: "her team recorded the faint traces of the dye at springs...."

B.why: You put a colon between "of" and its object, "the dye," which splits a prepositional phrase in half. A colon can only follow a complete thought, and "her team recorded the faint traces of" isn't one.

C.why: You put a dash right after "recorded," which cuts the verb off from its object. A single dash works like a colon, so everything before it must be a complete sentence. "Her team recorded" leaves out what was recorded.

D.why: You put a comma after "recorded," probably because the opening phrase "Over the next eleven weeks" made you expect another pause. A comma never separates a verb from its direct object.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

D.why: The colon earlier in the passage may have made a dash seem natural here. A single dash, like a colon, must follow a complete sentence. The long subject is not one yet, because its verb comes after the blank.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For decades, scholars assumed that the Czech composer Bohuslav Martinů abandoned the folk songs of his childhood after he moved to Paris in 1923. Musicologist Hana Dvořáková's study of his notebooks challenges that view. Her analysis shows how the composer continued to copy melodies from his home village into his sketchbooks ______ he disguised them by shifting their rhythms and stretching their phrases across new meters.
explanation: "Shows" has two objects joined by "and": "how the composer continued to copy melodies..." and "how he disguised them...." Two parallel parts of a sentence joined by "and" take no punctuation between them. Neither "how" clause can stand alone as a sentence.

B.why: The first "how" clause is long, so a comma before "and" felt like a natural breath. A comma plus "and" joins two complete sentences, though, and "how he disguised them..." isn't a sentence. It's the second object of "shows."

C.why: A semicolon must have a complete sentence on each side. "And how he disguised them by shifting their rhythms ..." is a fragment, so the semicolon is wrong.

D.why: You put a colon in the middle of a pair of objects. A colon introduces something the first part points to. Here the second "how" clause is just the other half of a list of two that "shows" already governs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Leaves record the air they grew in. When carbon dioxide levels are high, plants form fewer stomata, the tiny pores through which they take in gas. Paleobotanist Mirela Sandu used this relationship to estimate carbon dioxide levels during a warm period 56 million years ago. She could not use every fossil she collected, however. Only the leaf ______ preserved an unbroken outer layer of cells could be counted reliably.
explanation: "That preserved an unbroken outer layer of cells" is an essential clause. It tells you which impressions could be counted, and without it the sentence would claim that every leaf impression worked. Essential "that" clauses are never set off with punctuation. With no punctuation, the subject "Only the leaf impressions that preserved..." leads straight to its verb, "could be counted."

B.why: You put a comma before "that," which treats the clause as extra information. It's actually what picks out the usable fossils from the rest. A clause that begins with "that" is never set off by a comma.

C.why: You opened an interruption with a dash, but this clause isn't an interruption. It identifies the noun. Also, no second dash closes it before "could be counted," so the dash is unpaired as well as unneeded.

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. "Only the leaf impressions" has no verb, so the semicolon leaves a fragment on the left.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 1569 the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map on which any line of constant compass bearing appears perfectly straight, a property navigators prized. The trade-off was severe distortion at high latitudes, where Greenland swells until it seems to rival Africa in size. Yet the sailors and harbor pilots who relied on his projection for nearly three centuries of ocean ______ that distortion a small price for a course they could trust.
explanation: Cross out the long modifier "who relied on his projection for nearly three centuries of ocean crossings." What's left is "the sailors and harbor pilots ... considered that distortion a small price." The blank sits between a subject and its verb, and no punctuation can go between those two, however long the subject runs.

B.why: You took a breath after the long subject and put a comma there. A single comma can't separate a subject ("the sailors and harbor pilots") from its verb ("considered"). Length doesn't change that rule.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. Everything before the blank is a subject with no main verb, so that side is a fragment and the semicolon cuts the sentence apart.

D.why: A colon has to follow a complete sentence. The text before the blank never reaches its main verb, so there's nothing complete for the colon to introduce from.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: During the cholera outbreak of 1854, the London physician John Snow did not accept the popular theory that the disease spread through foul air. Snow—working decades before germ theory was established—set out to explain how the illness was moving through the Soho ______ why deaths clustered so tightly around a single public water pump on Broad Street. His map of those deaths is now regarded as a founding document of epidemiology.
explanation: Work out what "and" is joining. It links two parallel objects of "explain": "how the illness was moving" and "why deaths clustered." Neither one is a sentence that stands on its own here. Each is a clause the verb takes as its object. When "and" joins two parallel elements that aren't independent sentences, no punctuation goes before it.

B.why: You treated "and" as if it joined two complete sentences, which is when a comma before a FANBOYS word belongs. Here it joins two "how/why" objects of the same verb, so the comma breaks up the pair.

C.why: The dashes earlier in the sentence already open and close their interruption around "working decades before germ theory was established." A third dash at the blank has nothing to pair with, and it splits "explain" from its second object.

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. What follows the blank, "and why deaths clustered...," is a fragment that still depends on "explain."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before the 1930s, earthquakes were compared mainly by the damage they left behind, a measure that said as much about local building practices as about the shaking itself. Seismologist Charles Richter wanted a number drawn from instruments instead. The logarithmic ______ he and colleague Beno Gutenberg calibrated against readings from a standard seismometer let researchers rank quakes in distant regions on a single footing for the first time.
explanation: The "that" clause tells you which scale is meant: the one Richter and Gutenberg calibrated. It's essential to the noun, so it can't be set off with punctuation. It also sits inside a long subject whose verb is "let," so any mark at the blank would cut the subject apart before it reaches that verb.

B.why: You paused before "that" because the subject is long. An essential "that" clause is never separated from its noun by a comma, and this lone comma also never closes before the verb "let."

C.why: A colon has to come after a complete sentence. "The logarithmic scale" is only the start of a subject, so nothing complete stands before the colon.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon and needs a complete sentence before it. If you read it as opening an interruption, there's no second dash to close it before "let."

stimulus: Each day, roughly 900 stations around the world release weather balloons carrying instruments that radio back temperature, pressure, and humidity as they rise. The three-day forecasts built from the complete set and the three-day forecasts built from the reduced ______ by nearly 15 percent in accuracy.
explanation: The blank sits between a long subject ("The three-day forecasts built from the complete set and the three-day forecasts built from the reduced set") and its verb ("differed"). Cross out the long subject, and "The forecasts differed by nearly 15 percent" reads as one clean sentence.

B.why: You took a breath after the long subject and turned it into a comma. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject runs.

C.why: A semicolon has to have a complete sentence on each side. Neither side is one here: the first is only a subject and the second is only a verb phrase.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so the words before it have to form a complete sentence. They're only a subject without a verb, so the dash splits the sentence where it can't be split.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Planners in the city of Arlen compared two downtown corridors of similar length and traffic volume. One was redesigned in 2016 with separated bicycle lanes and the other was left unchanged. In its final report, the planning office singled out the ______ most of that difference: a curb-height concrete barrier between the bicycle lanes and car traffic.
explanation: "That explained most of that difference" tells you which feature the report means, so it is an essential clause. Without it, "singled out the feature" doesn't identify anything. Essential "that" clauses are never set off from their noun, so you need no punctuation. The colon later in the sentence is correct, because everything before it is now a complete clause.

A.why: You treated the "that" clause as extra information. It's what identifies the feature, and a comma never separates a noun from the essential "that" clause that defines it.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. "In its final report, the planning office singled out the feature" does stand alone, but "that explained most of that difference" does not, so the semicolon is wrong.

D.why: A dash would fence off the "that" clause as an interruption. The clause is essential to the noun, and this dash is never closed before the colon, so the punctuation around the interruption doesn't match.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In mokuhanga, the Japanese method of woodblock printing, every color is carved into its own block and pressed by hand onto damp paper. A finished landscape may pass under a dozen or more blocks, so each impression has to line up exactly with the ones before it. The small L-shaped notch called a kentō, cut into the same corner of every ______ the printer to set each sheet in precisely the same position.
explanation: The comma after "kentō" opens an interruption, "cut into the same corner of every block." A comma has to close it. Cross the interrupter out and you are left with "The small L-shaped notch called a kentō allows the printer to set each sheet...", which is a complete sentence with a single subject and verb. The opening comma needs a matching comma before "allows," and that comma marks where the interruption ends. It does not split the subject from its verb.

B.why: You were right not to want a breath pause between a subject and its verb. But you missed the comma after "kentō" much earlier, which opened an interruption. Without a closing comma, the interruption never ends and runs straight into the verb.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The small L-shaped notch... cut into the same corner of every block" has no main verb, and "allows the printer..." has no subject. Both sides are fragments.

D.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. The text before the blank is only a long subject still waiting for its verb, so a colon cuts the sentence apart at its core.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Many languages of the Andes use evidential suffixes, word endings that tell the listener how the speaker came to know something. A field linguist recording conversations in one highland Quechua community set out to measure both how often speakers chose the suffix marking direct observation ______ the suffix marking hearsay took its place as a story was retold from one household to the next.
explanation: The verb "measure" has two parallel objects, joined by "both... and": "how often speakers chose..." and "when the suffix marking hearsay took its place...". Neither one is a separate sentence. Both are noun clauses that complete "measure." When "and" joins two parallel parts like this, nothing goes between them, so no punctuation is correct.

A.why: The first object is long, so it feels like you need a pause before "and." But a comma with "and" joins two complete sentences. Here "and" pairs two objects of one verb, and the "both... and" construction makes that pairing explicit, so the comma has no job to do.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. What comes after the blank, "and when the suffix marking hearsay took its place...", cannot stand alone. It is the second half of a pair that belongs to "measure."

D.why: A colon introduces something that explains or lists what came before it. Here it would split the two halves of "both... and" and treat the second object as if it explained the first.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The peacock mantis shrimp smashes snail shells with a pair of club-shaped appendages, delivering one of the fastest strikes in the animal kingdom. Materials scientists studying the club have found that its outer layer is hard but brittle. They have therefore concentrated on the softer inner region, a stack of mineralized fibers arranged in a gradual spiral, and on the specific ______ the club from cracking apart after thousands of blows.
explanation: The clause "that keeps the club from cracking apart..." tells you which arrangement the scientists studied. It is essential to the meaning, and an essential "that" clause attaches to its noun with no punctuation. Read it as one unit: "the specific arrangement that keeps the club from cracking apart."

A.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it needs a complete sentence before it and something that explains that sentence after it. Here it splits a noun from the clause that defines it, which leaves "the specific arrangement" hanging with no meaning of its own.

B.why: The text before the blank seems to point ahead, so a colon feels like it is delivering an explanation. But "that keeps the club from cracking" is not a separate explanation. It is part of the noun phrase, and a colon cannot cut into a noun phrase.

C.why: A comma before "that" treats the clause as extra information that could be removed. A "that" clause is always essential, and without it "the specific arrangement" would not identify anything. Commas never separate a noun from its essential "that" clause.
